headline: High: shared filesystem and broad write/network capabilities make prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write filesystem content, and agent_a explicitly shares state via filesystem and git while agent_b uses workspace files and durable memory. That creates a default path for one agent to ingest the other's outputs as trusted content. No provenance or isolation mechanism is documented, so injection risk is real but not clearly high.
conditions: IF agent_a writes instructions into repo files or git-tracked content that agent_b later reads as context
IF agent_b ingests workspace files or memory entries produced by agent_a without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct workspaces
Disable automatic ingestion of repo files as instructions
Add a provenance tag to inter-agent handoff files
Review any shared markdown or task files before reuse
requires-engineering: enforce content-type or provenance filtering on shared channels

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent_a handles source code, git history, shell environment, and secrets in the invoking user's host session, while agent_b touches API keys, private keys, bearer tokens, and workspace files. Both have broad filesystem access and network egress, so sensitive data can move between them and out to external services by default. The pair lacks documented isolation or DLP controls.
conditions: IF either agent reads secrets from shared workspace files or environment variables
IF agent_b forwards workspace contents or memory to external APIs
IF agent_a exposes git history or shell environment to agent_b through shared files
mitigations: Move secrets out of shared directories
Use separate OS users or containers for each agent
Redact credentials before any file handoff
Restrict network egress for one or both agents
requires-engineering: add secret-scanning and DLP gates on shared files

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem, modify git state, spawn subprocesses, and use MCP. Agent_a shares state via filesystem and git; agent_b shares durable memory and workspace files. Concurrent edits to the same repo or workspace can overwrite each other or corrupt git state, and no locking is documented. This is a default conflict pathway.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or workspace path
IF either agent commits or rewrites git state while the other is active
IF shared MCP tools mutate the same external resource without locks
mitigations: Assign separate branches or worktrees
Serialize write operations with a lock file
Disable concurrent git commits
Use per-agent workspace directories
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency checks for shared resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent_b has many action surfaces and can run browsers, webhooks, and APIs; agent_a can produce code, shell commands, and git changes. If agent_b treats agent_a's output as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into external actions or commits. No verification step is documented between them, so the default pathway is dangerous.
conditions: IF agent_b executes or forwards agent_a-generated commands, code, or facts without verification
IF agent_a's suggested changes are committed or sent through agent_b's webhook/API surfaces
IF browser or webhook actions are triggered from unreviewed agent_a output
mitigations: Require human review before execution
Add a verification checklist for agent_a outputs
Block direct commit or send actions from untrusted text
Use a diff-only handoff format
requires-engineering: add automated validation of commands and facts

E_compliance.rationale: Agent_a is a closed-source terminal agent running on the host and handling git credentials; agent_b is an open-source assistant with broad workspace, webhook, and secret-handling surfaces. The pair can move sensitive code, credentials, or logs across different retention and residency regimes, but the profiles do not specify a concrete jurisdiction mismatch. The compliance risk is therefore moderate, not high.
conditions: IF regulated data such as credentials, logs, or customer records are placed into shared workspaces
IF one agent's logs or memory retain data longer than the other agent's policy
IF a deployment requires residency or certification alignment that the pair does not share
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces
Align retention settings before use
Document which agent may store which data class
Review webhook and audit-log retention
requires-engineering: map both agents to a common compliance boundary
